message.content:
Let \(p(n)=n^2-n+41\). Then

\[
p(n+1)=(n+1)^2-(n+1)+41=n^2+n+41.
\]

If \(d=\gcd(p(n),p(n+1))\), then \(d\mid p(n+1)-p(n)=2n\).

Also, \(p(n)=n(n-1)+41\) is always odd, so \(d\) cannot be even. Thus any common divisor greater than \(1\) must be an odd prime \(q\).

Since \(q\mid 2n\), we get \(q\mid n\). But \(q\mid p(n)=n^2-n+41\), and if \(q\mid n\), then \(q\mid 41\). Therefore the only possible common prime factor is

\[
q=41.
\]

So we need \(41\mid p(n)\) and \(41\mid p(n+1)\).

Modulo \(41\),

\[
p(n)\equiv n^2-n=n(n-1),
\]
\[
p(n+1)\equiv n^2+n=n(n+1).
\]

For both to be divisible by \(41\), we need

\[
n(n-1)\equiv 0 \pmod{41}
\]

and

\[
n(n+1)\equiv 0 \pmod{41}.
\]

The first gives \(n\equiv 0\) or \(1\pmod{41}\). The second gives \(n\equiv 0\) or \(-1\pmod{41}\). The only common possibility is

\[
n\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

The smallest positive such \(n\) is \(41\).

Indeed, \(p(41)=41^2=1681\) and \(p(42)=1763=41\cdot 43\), so they share factor \(41\).

The answer is 41.
